items.readable_text:
Content:
A discrete random variable [MATH: X] follows a discrete uniform distribution over a set [MATH: S] if each value in [MATH: S] is equally likely.

Content:
The probability mass function for the discrete uniform distribution on a set [MATH: S] is given by

Content:
[MATH: {(1)/(|S|),|x ∈ S,; 0,|otherwise.]

Content:
When a random variable [MATH: X] follows a discrete uniform distribution over the set [MATH: S=\{ s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\},] we denote it as

Content:
[MATH: X \sim U \left\{ s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\right\}]

Content:
and we say that [MATH: X] is uniformly distributed over [MATH: S.]

Content:
For example, consider the random variable [MATH: T\sim U\{1,2,4\}.] In this case, [MATH: S = \{1,2,4\},] [MATH: |S| = 3,] and therefore the probability mass function for [MATH: T] is

Content:
[MATH: {(1)/(3),|t ∈ {1, 2, 4},; 0,|otherwise.]

Content:
A sketch of [MATH: f(t)] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/15533b7daaabee0aafac7f3493427c98]

Content:
Note: In this lesson, we will make use of the following formula for computing the cardinality of a set of consecutive numbers:

Content:
[MATH: \left| \{ a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b \} \right| = b - a + 1]

Content:
Don't forget about the [MATH: +1] at the end of the formula. The [MATH: +1] is needed because we are including both endpoints [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] in the count. (Not convinced? Notice that [MATH: \left| \{ 4, 5 \} \right| = 5 - 4 + 1 = 2.])

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: X] follows a discrete uniform distribution over a set [MATH: S,] then [MATH: X] has the following probability mass function:

[MATH: {(1)/(|S|),|x ∈ S; 0,|otherwise]

Here, we have [MATH: X \sim U \left\lbrace 7, 8, 9, \ldots, 21 \right\rbrace,] and the set [MATH: S = \left\lbrace 7, 8, 9, \ldots, 21 \right\rbrace] has [MATH: |S|=21 - 7 + 1 = 15] items. So, we have

[MATH: {(1)/(15),|x = 7, 8, 9, …, 21; 0,|otherwise.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(X = 18) = f(18) = \dfrac{1}{15}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
[MATH: X \sim U \left\{ s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\right\}]

Content:
and we say that [MATH: X] is uniformly distributed over [MATH: S.]

Content:
For example, consider the random variable [MATH: T\sim U\{1,2,4\}.] In this case, [MATH: S = \{1,2,4\},] [MATH: |S| = 3,] and therefore the probability mass function for [MATH: T] is
